approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop-to-Carbon traverse under Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
The traditional approach was the Carbon River road to Ipsut Creek and up the Carbon Glacier. Carbon River access has been interrupted for long stretches by bridge and road failure on the state highway that serves it, and when it is out the Carbon side becomes a very long wilderness walk rather than a drive-in. Treat that as a thing to confirm rather than a fixed fact in either direction.

The approach most parties now use starts at White River Campground: Glacier Basin Trail to Glacier Basin, climbers' path to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, then rope up, drop onto the Winthrop and traverse west and around beneath Curtis Ridge onto the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft.

From the Carbon, walk up under the wall. Bivy sites exist in the Curtis Ridge access gully and on Curtis Ridge itself.

This is one of the most objectively dangerous pieces of ground in the range. The whole wall is capped by the summit icecap and swept by what comes off it. Nothing in the rack protects you from that; being there in the cold hours does.
approach_variants.season: Cold, hard-frozen conditions only — a narrow and unpredictable late-spring window, and the route is more often not in condition than in it
hazards: Extreme objective hazard from the hanging summit icecap seracs, along the entire wall
Continuous rockfall down the face
No easy retreat once committed; a long, serious approach on both sides
Crevassed glacier travel on the Winthrop and Carbon, and again on the summit icecap above
Carbon River road access is intermittently severed, which changes the approach from a drive-in to a multi-day walk
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE TEST IS WHAT IS ABOVE YOU, NOT WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU. Willis Wall is capped along its entire top by the hanging summit ice cliff, and all three of its ribs rise from the base of the wall directly above the Carbon Glacier, underneath that cliff. If you are standing beneath a face that is NOT capped by a continuous ice cliff, you are not under Willis Wall. THE TWO WAYS TO BE WRONG ARE ON OPPOSITE SIDES, AND THE RIDGES NAME THEM. Willis Wall is bounded by CURTIS RIDGE on one side and LIBERTY RIDGE on the other. Facing the wall from the Carbon Glacier, Curtis Ridge is the rib you came around to get here and Liberty Ridge is the rib beyond the far edge of the wall. If you have walked past Liberty Ridge you are under Liberty Wall, which is a different wall with a different reputation. COUNT THE GLACIERS: TWO. Winthrop, then Carbon. One means you stopped at Curtis Ridge. THE ROUTE DOES NOT NAME A RIB, AND THAT IS THE FACT TO CARRY IN. This wall carries three distinct ribs, climbed in different years by different parties and of materially different character. Which one you are under is a decision to be made at the base, from photographs taken before you left, and not something the approach settles for you. Do not treat 'the base of Willis Wall' as though it were one start. WHAT BEING TOO LATE LOOKS LIKE: nothing visual. The wall does not change. Time of day is the variable that kills here, so the honest base finding is that arriving under it after the sun has been on the icecap means turning round, not looking harder for the rib.

before.overview: The Ingraham Direct is the early-season twin of the Disappointment Cleaver, climbing straight up the Ingraham Glacier headwall beneath the Ingraham icefall instead of detouring onto the Cleaver's rock rib. It's usually in best shape from late May through June while the headwall is still filled and continuous; NPS climbing rangers steer parties onto the Disappointment Cleaver once the bergschrund opens and rockfall/icefall exposure from the serac band above increases.
before.approach: The Ingraham Direct on Mount Rainier begins at Paradise (5,400 ft). Follow the paved Skyline Trail through subalpine meadows and past Panorama Point (~5-7 hours) to Camp Muir (10,080 ft), gaining 4,000 ft. Above Camp Muir, traverse the heavily crevassed Ingraham Glacier—rope-team travel mandatory. A hard overnight freeze is essential for safe glacier travel; start the summit push at 1-2 AM to climb the final 3,400 ft while snow is firm. Non-technical but exposed; the crux is route-finding through crevasse fields and steep snowfield sections.

From the Mowich Lake trailhead (reached via the Mowich Lake Road, which typically opens later in the season than White River Road), follow the Wonderland Trail roughly 3-4 miles through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Wonderland Trail begins to descend toward the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. Continue ascending the ridge's lower apron until it narrows above Observation Rock; established bivy sites (some with old wind-break rock walls) sit around 9,600-10,300 ft near the base of the North Mowich/Edmunds Glaciers, used as camps for Mowich Face, Edmunds Headwall, and Ptarmigan Ridge alike. From camp, drop and traverse across the North Mowich Glacier (roped, watch for recent rockfall debris crossing the ice) to gain the base of the Mowich Face proper. This is a genuinely long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds — self-sufficiency and solid navigation are required, and there's no water above Spray Park except melted snow.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan Ridge camp, then across the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and seasonal. In a normal year it opens well after the roads on the east and south sides of the park — commonly not until July — and closes with the first significant snow. Access to it along the state highway from the north has also been interrupted by bridge failure for extended periods, in which case Mowich Lake itself becomes a long wilderness walk from another park entrance. Confirm which of those two situations applies before you commit a trip to this side.

From Mowich Lake, follow the Wonderland Trail roughly 3-4 miles through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Wonderland begins to descend toward the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast BETWEEN ECHO ROCK AND OBSERVATION ROCK, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge.

Camps sit on the ridge between roughly 9,600 and 10,300 ft, some with old rock wind walls; these serve the Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall and Ptarmigan Ridge alike. From camp you DROP and traverse the North Mowich Glacier, roped, watching for fresh rockfall debris on the ice, to gain the base of the face.

There is no water above Spray Park and no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds of this approach.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for ice; the face bares out and starts shedding rock as it warms
hazards: Sustained steep ice and snow with multiple line options and no obvious separation between them

approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO NAMED ROCKS ARE THE ONLY HARD MARKERS ON THE WHOLE CROSS-COUNTRY SECTION, AND THEY WORK IN CLOUD BECAUSE THEY ARE BIG AND THEY ARE A PAIR. You leave the Wonderland Trail and go BETWEEN ECHO ROCK AND OBSERVATION ROCK. Not past one of them — between the two. If you can only see one rock, you do not yet know which one it is.

THE SECOND THING IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IT IS WHERE PARTIES GO WRONG: FROM HIGH CAMP YOU GO DOWN. Camp is on Ptarmigan Ridge; the face is across the North Mowich Glacier from it. If you leave camp and start climbing, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge, which is a different route to a different top-out. Losing height off the ridge is correct and is the single clearest signal that you are on this climb and not its neighbour.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE ARRIVAL AND IT IS FREQUENTLY NOT PASSABLE DIRECT. It has to be turned, so budget time for looking rather than treating the schrund as a formality. Reaching a schrund you cannot cross straight over means you are probably in the right place.

THIS IS THE UMBRELLA FACE, NOT A SINGLE LINE, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO CARRY IN. Four separate climbs share this wall and this camp — the North Mowich Headwall, the Central Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall, and Ptarmigan Ridge above and to the side of them. They are told apart by WHICH GLACIER you cross from camp and by WHAT THE FIRST GROUND ABOVE THE SCHRUND IS, not by the walk in, which is identical for all of them. Decide which one you are doing before you leave camp in the dark; there is roughly 4,000 ft of 40 to 55 degree ice and mixed ground above, and being one line out is not a thing you discover early.

WHAT RETREAT LOOKS LIKE, BECAUSE IT IS NOT THE WAY YOU CAME: there is no walk-off from the top of this face. Topping out commits you to a carryover down the far side of the mountain to Paradise or White River and a shuttle back. Backing off means reversing the North Mowich Glacier, climbing about 1,000 ft of scree and talus near Observation Rock, and walking out through Spray Park.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the bivy between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Mowich Face approach and is shared with three other climbs: Mowich Lake, the Wonderland Trail through Spray Park, then cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock onto the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge.

The bivouac for this route sits at roughly 9,600 to 10,000 ft on the divide BETWEEN the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers. Two days to reach it is the normal plan rather than a cautious one.

From the bivy the climbing starts almost at once. Above the hourglass, roughly 2,000 ft of about 45-degree snow leads to a rock band; the documented way through is to look for an arch in the rock on the right, traverse left, then work back right to gain the ice cap. In a low-snow year that band can demand unprotected loose 5th-class climbing, which is the part of this route that changes most from season to season.

Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and typically opens around July, and highway access from the north has been severed for extended periods. Confirm before committing.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, climbed early in the day for rockfall
hazards: A rock band crux that can require unprotected loose 5th-class climbing in low-snow years
Sustained steep ice with rockfall exposure — climb it early

approach_variants.baseFinding:
FOUR CLIMBS SHARE THIS WALL AND THIS CAMP. From the divide bivy the discriminator is WHICH GLACIER YOU CROSS AND WHERE THE HOURGLASS IS.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE STRONG ONE: THIS ROUTE'S HOURGLASS IS LOW. Within 40 to 50 ft of leaving the bivy you should be in a STEEP CONSTRICTION OF MIXED ROCK AND ICE. First ground, immediately, right off the deck. That is the North Mowich Headwall's signature.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS MOST IS THE CENTRAL MOWICH FACE NEXT DOOR, AND IT ALSO HAS AN HOURGLASS — BUT AT 12,500 FT, NOT AT 10,000. So the question at the base is not 'is there an hourglass on this route' but 'is the hourglass HERE, NOW, in the first 50 ft'. If your first 2,000 ft is open snow with no constriction at all, you are on the Central Mowich Face and your hourglass is still two thousand feet above you.

THE OTHER NEGATIVE IS THE EDMUNDS HEADWALL, AND IT IS SETTLED BY THE SCHRUND: the Edmunds is entered by bypassing its bergschrund on climber's LEFT near a pair of TWIN GENDARMES. If you crossed the schrund beside two rock towers, you are on the Edmunds and you crossed the wrong glacier out of camp.

SEQUENCE CHECK ONCE COMMITTED, IN ORDER: 40-50 ft hourglass of rock and ice, then roughly 2,000 ft of sustained 45-degree snow, then a rock band that has to be cleared. If the rock band arrives early, you are not on this line. If it never arrives, you traversed off onto the Central Mowich, which skirts the band entirely by going right.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR ROUND LOOKS LIKE: if you left camp and CLIMBED rather than crossing a glacier, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge.

approach_variants.name: White River Campground, Glacier Basin, Inter Glacier and Camp Schurman
approach_variants.notes:
The Glacier Basin trailhead is in Loop D of White River Campground (about 4,300–4,400 ft), reached by the White River road off SR 410. That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.1 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache. This is the last reliable water and the last forested camp.

Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft. The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow; it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard. It leads to Camp Curtis on the rim at about 8,500–9,000 ft.

From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow. There is an NPS ranger hut, an emergency radio on the front of it, toilets and a blue-bag barrel; tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.

Camp Schurman's nightly capacity is small — far smaller than Camp Muir's — so a permit here is worth reserving. The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight.
approach_variants.season: Late spring through August, once the White River road and campground are open and before summer melt opens the upper crevasse fields
hazards: Crevasses on the Inter Glacier, which open through the season despite its mild reputation
Loose, brittle volcanic rock on the direct scramble down the Prow into Camp Schurman
Rockfall onto the moraine path above Glacier Basin
Crevasse maze above 12,000 ft where the Corridor ends

Creek crossings and old slide paths on the Glacier Basin trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Three recognition points, in order.

At 0.9 mile from the trailhead there is a signed junction where the Emmons Moraine Trail branches LEFT and crosses the Inter Fork on a seasonal footbridge. If you cross a bridge over the river this early, you have left the climbers' route. The way to Glacier Basin stays right, on the old mining road grade, and does not cross the river there.

The start of glacier travel is the toe of the Inter Glacier, roughly a mile past Glacier Basin and about 7,000 ft. You get there by following the moraine crest; the test is that the ground turns from rubble and moraine to continuous snow, and there is no more path. Rope up when it does.

Camp Schurman is the third. It sits at the foot of Steamboat Prow, on the saddle where the Emmons and Winthrop split, with a hut on it. If you have topped out on the Prow's rocky summit you are ABOVE camp — there is a short, steep, very loose scramble down the front of the Prow to the huts, and the more usual line drops from Camp Curtis onto the lower Emmons and comes at the camp along the Prow's southern side instead. Coming back down in cloud, the Prow is the handrail: keep it on your side and you will find the camp.

Above camp the climbing starts as soon as you step off the platform — the first thing under your boots is the Emmons. The feature to find is the Corridor: a smooth, wide ramp of about 30 degrees trending slightly east, running from camp up to roughly 12,000 ft. The test is smoothness. If the slope you are on is broken by parallel crevasse trains and you are already end-running, you have drifted out of the Corridor into the icefall on either side of it. Above 12,000 ft the smooth ground ends and the glacier does become a maze — that is expected, not a sign you are lost. The bergschrund is crossed near 13,000 ft, and late in the season it can force a long traverse onto the upper Winthrop toward Liberty Saddle.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and lower Ptarmigan Ridge, then 1,000 ft down to the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Wonderland Trail from Mowich Lake about 4 miles to Spray Park, then the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge. At about 8,300 ft the route DESCENDS roughly 1,000 ft onto the North Mowich Glacier and crosses to the base of the face.

There are two lines from about 12,500 ft. The original variation cuts LEFT into an hourglass of snow, ice and rock, gaining a ledge that leads to a 40-50 degree ramp to the top. The harder variation cuts RIGHT through a couple of AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow to the same high point.

Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and typically opens around July; highway access to it from the north has been severed for long periods. Confirm current access before planning around this trailhead.
hazards: Ice steps and steep snow with rockfall exposure
A 1,000 ft descent onto the glacier on the approach, which must be reclimbed if you retreat
Remote approach with limited bailout options
Crevasses on the North Mowich crossing
Seasonal and intermittently severed road access on this side of the park
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT IS THAT YOU LOSE A THOUSAND FEET ON THE WAY IN. At about 8,300 ft on lower Ptarmigan Ridge you stop climbing and drop onto the North Mowich Glacier. A party that keeps gaining height is on Ptarmigan Ridge, not on this face, and will not find out for hours.

FOUR CLIMBS COME OFF THIS WALL AND THEY ARE SEPARATED BY WHERE THE STEEP GROUND IS, NOT BY THE WALK IN.

THE POSITIVE TEST FOR THIS ROUTE IS AN ABSENCE, WHICH IS UNUSUAL BUT IT IS THE RELIABLE ONE HERE: THERE IS NO CONSTRICTION LOW DOWN. You cross the schrund and climb open face. The hourglass on this route is HIGH — around 12,500 ft — not at the bottom. So if your first 50 ft above the schrund is a steep pinch of mixed rock and ice, you are on the North Mowich Headwall and you crossed too far round.

THE ROCK BAND SETTLES IT DEFINITIVELY, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE THE TWO LINES BEHAVE OPPOSITELY. On this face, at the rock band you can TRAVERSE RIGHT SEVERAL HUNDRED FEET AND SKIRT THE BAND ENTIRELY. On the North Mowich Headwall you cannot: you have to clear the band, at 5th class in a lean year. If the band in front of you has to be climbed rather than walked around, you are one line over.

SCHRUND CHECK: the bergschrund under the central face has been passed by a bypass through a rock band on climber's LEFT. If the only way across in front of you is beside a pair of twin gendarmes, that is the Edmunds Headwall's schrund and you are further round the mountain than you meant to be.

CHOOSE YOUR VARIATION BEFORE 12,500 FT, NOT AT IT. Left is the original: an hourglass, a ledge, a 40-50 degree ramp. Right is harder: AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow. They rejoin, but you cannot swap once you are on one.

before.approach: The road to Mowich Lake is closed indefinitely: WSDOT permanently closed the Fairfax Bridge on SR 165 on April 22, 2025, and the park's road-status page (updated September 18, 2026) lists no public access to Mowich Lake from SR 165, so the White River side is the only start a car can reach. Historically approached either from the west via Mowich Lake (shorter) or from the east via White River Campground (longer, typically requiring a car shuttle or carryover with descent via the Emmons Glacier). Which of the two is actually available is a seasonal question rather than a fixed one: the Mowich Lake road is summer-only and in a normal year opens well after this route comes into condition, so the shorter approach and the season rarely line up. The White River side is reachable earlier, at the cost of a much longer walk. Check the road status before planning around Mowich Lake.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park
approach_variants.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. The Mowich Lake road is unpaved, seasonal and typically opens later than the White River road — mid-summer rather than late spring in a normal snow year. Since the route is best when there is still winter snow on it, the road schedule is a structural problem with this variant rather than an occasional inconvenience. Check the road's status before planning around it.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake is closed indefinitely, so this start cannot currently be reached by car
hazards: Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Committing position with a descent by a different route — plan the carry-over
approach_variants.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you DESCEND, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
approach_variants.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers
Long committing traverse with no quick exit
Same bergschrund and upper mixed-ground hazards as the Mowich approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

before.detailed_rack: Light alpine technical rack: two tools, several ice screws, pickets, a single rope for running belays, full crevasse-rescue kit.
before.beta: A terraced buttress climb with 40-55° snow, mixed rock/snow/ice, and a bergschrund crossing low on the route; steeper and slightly more sustained than its neighbor Liberty Ridge, with a lower start-elevation summit push (~9,800 ft vs. Liberty Ridge's 10,700 ft from Thumb Rock).
before.watch_out:
Bergschrund crossing requires finding bridge just left of rock outcropping - end-run may be necessary if impassable
Icefall danger: climbing between rock buttress (right) and icefall (left) with angles 45-55 degrees
Hanging ice cliff nicknamed 'doom cliff' - serious objective hazard
One short vertical rock step with one or two fixed pins - may be missing or unreliable
Condition-dependent: may encounter almost entirely snow climb OR substantial climbing on verglassed rock and water ice
Requires ice screws, pins, and rock gear depending on conditions encountered
Sustained steep snow climbing 40-55 degrees on ~1000 ft summit day gain
High elevation remote position on northwest side
Limited bivy sites until reaching Liberty Cap Glacier
Steeper and more sustained than adjacent Liberty Ridge - demands experienced fit climbers

road.name: Westside Road
road.status: Gated to vehicles at mile 3 (Dry Creek Trailhead) due to repeated Tahoma Creek flooding/debris flows; gravel beyond the gate
road.driveNote: Park at the gate and hike the road to the Tahoma Creek Trail.
road.seasonalGate: Open to vehicles roughly May–November only as far as the mile-3 Dry Creek gate; the remaining ~13 miles to the Tahoma Creek/St. Andrews approach are foot/bike travel only

before.season: Best June-August; west aspect holds firmer snow later into the morning than south-facing routes

approach_variants.name: Westside Road and Tahoma Creek to St Andrews Rock, then the Sickle
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate at the Dry Creek trailhead near 2,900 ft. The road is gated to vehicles a few miles in because of repeated Tahoma Creek flooding and debris flows; the remainder is walked or biked, and has been for years. Plan the road as part of the climb.

From the gate, take the Tahoma Creek Trail up to the Wonderland Trail near 5,600 ft, then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier. Camps are used near Emerald Ridge lower down and around 9,800-10,400 ft near St Andrews Rock.

The glacier is climbed with a series of diagonal traverses: zigzag the south side to about 7,200 ft, then traverse back and forth around 9,000-10,000 ft to get through crevasse bands, then into the Sickle and out onto the plateau near 12,600 ft.

Car-to-car this is a very long outing — a documented itinerary from the road closure ran about 21.5 miles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, best in June; a west aspect that holds firmer snow later into the morning than the south-side routes
hazards: Complex crevasse navigation with several bands that have to be traversed around
Serac and icefall hazard in and below the Sickle, with unavoidable run-out exposure on the traverse
A long road walk at both ends and a very long car-to-car day
Route-finding on a committing west-side approach with no maintained trail above 5,600 ft
Thin late-season snow bridges over the upper glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ST ANDREWS ROCK IS THE RECOGNITION POINT, AND THE THING THAT CONFIRMS IT IS THAT YOU GO DOWN.

You climb to a ridge just short of 10,000 ft BELOW ST ANDREWS ROCK, and then you DROP several hundred feet on a ramp onto the Tahoma Glacier proper at around 9,600 ft. Losing that height is correct. It is the clearest single signal that you are on this route: a party that never gives height back has stayed on the Puyallup Cleaver and is heading for Sunset Ridge, one drainage north.

THE SICKLE IS THE SECOND MARKER AND IT IS A SHAPE, NOT A PLACE. At about 11,200 ft the route enters a NARROW CHUTE THAT CURVES LEFT AROUND A CLIFF — the reason it is called the Sickle. If you are climbing straight up open glacier with no constriction and no cliff to curve around, you are still below it, whatever the altimeter says.

CLIMB THE SICKLE ON ITS NORTH SIDE, KEEPING LEFT OF THE ICY RIDGES, to the plateau at about 12,600 ft. Topping the Sickle is the point at which you are out of the icefall run-out, and that is the honest marker for 'the dangerous part is behind you'.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR TIMING RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the traverse below the Sickle runs under its run-out zone, which funnels ice debris. There is no line through that avoids it. Being there in the dark and frozen is the only protection, so if you arrive at the base of the Sickle in the sun, the finding is that you should not be there, not that you should look for a better line.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE LOW DOWN: the route works the SOUTHERN side of the glacier from the Wonderland Trail at 5,600 ft. Drifting north early puts you into the crevasse bands the diagonal traverses exist to avoid.

before.approach: From Paradise (5,400 ft), follow the Skyline Trail up past Panorama Point and Pebble Creek onto the Muir Snowfield, climbing roughly 4.5 miles and about 4,700 ft to Camp Muir (10,080 ft) — the standard high camp for this route as well as the Disappointment Cleaver and Ingraham Direct routes. There is a seasonal water source at Pebble Creek lower on the Skyline Trail, but nothing reliable above it; melt snow at Camp Muir. From Camp Muir, the technical route begins almost immediately: cross the upper Cowlitz Glacier (roped) toward the Cowlitz Cleaver, then gain the ledge system running along the southern flank of Gibraltar Rock. These ledges are the crux — narrow, sometimes icy, and exposed — and connect to the Gibraltar Chute, a roughly 50° snow slope dropping to the Nisqually Glacier. Rockfall is the dominant hazard on the ledges themselves; this is a route to move through quickly, ideally while the rock is still frozen in the early morning.

climbing_route.label: Upper Cowlitz Glacier to the Cowlitz Cleaver
climbing_route.notes: From Camp Muir the technical route begins almost immediately: cross the upper Cowlitz Glacier roped, toward the Cowlitz Cleaver.

climbing_route.label: Gibraltar Ledges
climbing_route.notes: Gain the ledge system running along the southern flank of Gibraltar Rock. These ledges are the crux — narrow, sometimes icy, and exposed. Rockfall is the dominant hazard on the ledges themselves; move through quickly, ideally while the rock is still frozen in the early morning.

climbing_route.label: Gibraltar Chute
climbing_route.notes: The ledges connect to the Gibraltar Chute, a roughly 50° snow slope dropping to the Nisqually Glacier.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed in cold winter/spring conditions when the rock is frozen in place; becomes more hazardous with rockfall as the season warms.

days.note: Hike the Muir Snowfield to Camp Muir and settle in and rest for an early departure.
days.title: Paradise to Camp Muir
days.objective: Reach Camp Muir (10,080 ft)

days.note: Depart very early (often before dawn, sometimes as early as 12:30 AM) to cross the upper Cowlitz Glacier and Cowlitz Cleaver, then the ledges themselves before the sun hits the loose rock, reaching the crater rim and descending the DC to Paradise.
days.title: Summit day

schedule.label: Leave Camp Muir
schedule.detail: As early as 12:30 AM in cold/winter conditions

schedule.label: Cross the upper Cowlitz Glacier to the Cowlitz Cleaver
Traverse Gibraltar Ledges
schedule.detail: Loose rock — climbed before the sun hits it, ~5 hrs Muir to the top of the ledges

schedule.label: Descend DC to Muir, continue to Paradise

days.objective: Traverse the ledges and summit

itinerary.totalNote: A standard 2-day trip (~9,000 ft gain); now considered the standard winter/shoulder-season route, so an early, cold departure is essential to beat rockfall on the ledges.

before.overview: The historic 1870 Stevens-Van Trump first-ascent route, traversing exposed ledges beneath the cliff of Gibraltar Rock on the south side. From Camp Muir the route ascends the western edge of the Cowlitz Glacier below the Cowlitz Cleaver, passes beneath a rock feature called the Beehive, and crosses the cleaver through a notch near Cathedral Rocks to reach the base of Gibraltar Rock. From about 11,800 ft the route follows exposed snow-and-rock 'ledges' along the base of Gibraltar Rock for roughly a third of a mile to the top of Gibraltar Chute (~12,600 ft, sometimes called 'Camp Comfort'); the crux is an ice chute between Gibraltar Rock and the upper Nisqually ice cliff leading to the saddle. From there it's a sustained ~2,000 ft push to the east crater rim and across the crater to the true summit.

approach_variants.name: Paradise to Camp Muir, then the Cowlitz Cleaver
approach_variants.notes:
Paradise (5,420 ft) to Camp Muir (10,080 ft) by the Skyline Trail and the Muir Snowfield, the same carry as the Disappointment Cleaver. Pebble Creek (~7,200 ft) is the last running water; melt snow at Muir. Because this is a cold-season route the snowfield is very often a compass problem — unmarked, unmaintained, glaciers on both flanks, and a corniced cliff band between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock. The Park Service's published bearing from Pebble Creek to Moon Rocks is 355 degrees true.

Some parties carry past Muir to a camp near 10,800 ft on the cleaver, which shortens the summit day and gets you above the first section.

This route is short on approach and long on exposure: unlike the Cleaver and the Ingraham Direct, the technical ground starts within minutes of leaving the tent. The ledges face southwest and stay in shade until roughly mid-morning, which is the whole timing argument — the ledges and the chute above them are a rockfall funnel once the sun reaches them, and the route is only recommended when everything up there is frozen.
approach_variants.season: Winter and spring, while snow and ice cover the ledges; documented into early June
hazards: Rockfall onto the ledges and into the Gibraltar Chute once the sun reaches the southwest aspect
Exposed, narrow, sometimes icy traverse with no easy retreat once committed
Whiteout navigation on the Muir Snowfield in winter conditions
Large crevasses separating the top of the route from the glacier above
Avalanche hazard on the cleaver and in the chute after loading
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You leave camp and you are on the route. There is no walk-in phase, which is exactly why people get this one wrong in the dark.

The start is the ridgeline immediately northwest of Camp Muir — the Cowlitz Cleaver. Not east across the Cowlitz Glacier: east is Cathedral Gap and the Disappointment Cleaver, the opposite side of camp. If the first thing you are doing is a roped glacier traverse away from the huts toward a rock notch, you have turned the wrong way out of Muir.

On the cleaver you gain roughly 1,600 ft of moderate to steep snow, threading around rock gendarmes, passing beneath the Beehive and crossing the crest through a notch. The section ends where it runs into the base of Gibraltar Rock at about 11,800 ft — that is unmistakable, a large rock mass you cannot go through.

The ledges are the confirmation. At the base of Gib Rock you should find an exposed shelf of snow and rock that traverses horizontally along the rock's southwest-facing base for about a third of a mile. If you are climbing rather than traversing, you have not found the ledge system. The ledges deliver you to the foot of the Gibraltar Chute, and the chute is about 400 ft of 45-degree snow ending at the top of Gibraltar Rock at roughly 12,300 ft. Above that, most parties trend onto the upper Ingraham for another 1,200 ft to avoid crevasses and join the standard route near 13,800 ft.

The timing test matters as much as the location test: you want to be across the ledges and out of the chute before the sun hits that southwest aspect.
